claim: Greater hippocampal activity while viewing new photos predicted later memory-based looking, beginning around 1 year of age
quote: Greater activity in the hippocampus during the viewing of previously unseen photographs was related to later memory-based looking behavior beginning around 1 year of age

claim: Encoding-test lag averaged 59.9 s with 3-12 intervening items, putting the task outside working memory
quote: The lag between encoding and test (mean = 59.9 s, SD = 15.8 s) and the interruption by intervening trials (3 to 12 items) place the memory demands of this task outside of the range of working memory.

claim: Each item was shown once for only 2 s at encoding, which favours familiarity rather than novelty preferences
quote: Such familiarity preferences are more likely when a stimulus is not fully habituated, as was likely in our study because items were presented only once during encoding and very briefly (2 s) by infant standards

claim: 26 infants aged 4.2-24.9 months, half younger and half older than 1 year, provided usable data
quote: We collected usable awake fMRI data and anatomical scans from 26 infants aged 4.2 to 24.9 months of age

claim: There was no overall familiarity preference in the full sample (mean 0.510 vs 0.5)
quote: We did not find an overall familiarity preference (proportion of test trials with more looking to old item) in the full sample

claim: Familiarity preference did not differ between age groups nor vary with continuous age
quote: there was also neither a difference between age groups

claim: Whole-hippocampus BOLD was greater for later-preferred items (mean z = 0.295, P = 0.008)
quote: There was significantly greater BOLD activity in the whole hippocampus during the encoding of items for which infants later showed a familiarity preference versus items for which

claim: The effect was significant in posterior but not anterior hippocampus, though the difference between them was not significant
quote: This subsequent memory effect was evident in the posterior hippocampus

claim: The posterior-anterior difference itself did not reach significance
quote: the comparison between posterior and anterior did not reach significance

claim: Results were not explained by item memorability or serial position confounds
quote: such as item effects or memorability (fig. S2) or serial position (fig. S3)

claim: Hippocampal activity was unrelated to general strength of test preference when old and new preferences were combined
quote: hippocampal activity at encoding was unrelated to the general strength of the test preference when preferences for the old and new items were combined

claim: The effect was robust in infants with above-median familiarity preference and unreliable in those below
quote: The hippocampal subsequent memory effect was robust in infants with a higher average familiarity preference

claim: The whole-hippocampus effect was driven by older infants (12-24 months), with none in 4-9-month-olds
quote: The subsequent memory effect in the whole hippocampus was driven by the older infants

claim: Age also predicted the effect continuously (Spearman r = 0.385, P = 0.034)
quote: it was also evident when age in months was considered as a continuous variable

claim: The age effect survived partialling out six age-related confounds including usable trials, attention and hippocampal volume
quote: partialing out six potential age-related confounds, including measures of the number of usable trials, attention to the screen, looking preferences, and hippocampal volume

claim: Hippocampal activity variance (noise) was comparable between older and younger infants
quote: we confirmed that the variance in hippocampal activity (as a measure of noise) was comparable between older and younger infants

claim: All three categories showed the pattern; objects were most reliable, then scenes
quote: objects were the most reliable, followed by scenes

claim: In older infants the effect was clearer for shorter study-test lags
quote: the subsequent memory effect in the whole hippocampus for older infants was clearer for shorter than longer study-test lags

claim: Whole-brain: older infants showed effects in bilateral hippocampus and right orbitofrontal cortex; younger showed none
quote: older infants showed effects in the bilateral hippocampus (P < 0.01, uncorrected) and in the right orbitofrontal cortex (P < 0.05, corrected)

claim: No clear MTL cortex (entorhinal, perirhinal, parahippocampal) involvement, unlike adults
quote: Yet, we did not observe clear involvement of the MTL cortex in the wholebrain analysis or in ROIs that encompassed entorhinal, perirhinal, and parahippocampal cortices

claim: Younger and older infants did not differ in behavioural looking preferences, arguing against a performance account
quote: Younger and older infants did not differ in their overall behavioral looking preferences

claim: Stimulus duration was fixed, complicating the age effect given developmental change in encoding time
quote: stimulus duration was fixed in the current study, which may complicate the interpretation of age effects given developmental changes in the time needed for encoding

claim: Tentative evidence that posterior hippocampus participates in retrieval in older infants (test trials)
quote: we found tentative evidence that the posterior hippocampus may be involved in memory retrieval in older infants

claim: Episodic encoding only after 12 months contrasts with hippocampal statistical learning from ~3 months, consistent with later trisynaptic vs monosynaptic pathway development
quote: episodic encoding in the current study was observed only in infants older than 12 months, whereas statistical learning has been observed in the hippocampus throughout infancy, starting at around 3 months

claim: Onset near 1 year is earlier than predictions from spatial memory and structural development in nonhuman animals
quote: though it is earlier than predictions based on spatial memory and structural development in nonhuman animals

claim: Implication: postencoding mechanisms (retrieval inaccessibility) rather than encoding failure may be more responsible for infantile amnesia
quote: implies that postencoding mechanisms, whereby memories from infancy become inaccessible for retrieval, may be more responsible for infantile amnesia

claim: Rodent dorsal hippocampus, homologous to human posterior, holds infant engrams that persist but are inaccessible
quote: memory engrams formed during infancy in the dorsal hippocampus, homologous to the posterior hippocampus in humans, can persist into adulthood but remain inaccessible at retrieval without direct stimulation
